records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox page for Humulus lupulus (the only admissible page read). Its Poison block sits under the human-scoped heading 'Poisonous to Humans': Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "SKIN IRRITATION MINOR, OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Skin irritation with blisters upon contact. Dogs: panting, high body temperature, seizures, death."; Poison Toxic Principle: "Volatile oils and bitter acids"; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part: Flowers, Leaves (the full two-part list). The page header reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Handling warning, from the page's plant-problems text: "Contact with skin can cause dermatitis in some." Separately from the Poison block, the Problems field lists Contact Dermatitis, Problem for Dogs and Weedy, the tag line includes #problem for dogs and #contact dermatitis, and Plant Type is Herbaceous Perennial, Vine. The pet evidence is dog-only: the 'Dogs:' symptom line and the Problem for Dogs tag name dogs, and the page says nothing about cats, so no risk to cats is recorded either way and the dog signs must not be generalized to cats or people. Edibility is part-specific: the Edibility field reads "Fruiting cones used for brewing beer.", the Uses (Ethnobotany) field says "Extract from the fruit bracts are used as a flavoring in the production of beer.", and the Fruit Description ends "They are used in making beer."; the Description instead says the plant is grown commercially for its seeds, used as the brewing flavoring. The listed poison parts are the flowers and leaves. is_edible true covers the cones for brewing beer only; it does not mean the flowers, the leaves or the plant as a whole are safe to eat.
unknowns: Only NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) loaded for this exact name; MoBot, RHS, Clemson and the other admissible domains could not be read here (connection errors, 404, 403 on guessed URLs), so no cross-source check was possible and no second source backs any field.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source read addresses indoor growing; NC State presents it as an outdoor herbaceous climbing vine (Plant Type: Herbaceous Perennial, Vine; USDA zones 5a-8b) that needs a fence, wall, trellis or pergola to climb.
toxic_to_pets is true on dog evidence only (NC State 'Problem for Dogs' and the Dogs symptom line); the page says nothing about cats.

NC State's Poison block (severity Low, dermatitis) is human-scoped; the dog signs (panting, high body temperature, seizures, death) are a separate dog line and must not be generalized to people or cats.

Edibility is conditional: NC State says fruiting cones are used for brewing beer; flowers and leaves are the listed poison parts. The page's description paragraph says 'seeds' are used as the flavoring while the Edibility and Uses fields say cones/fruit bracts; this internal wording difference is unresolved.

soil_drainage moderate comes from NC State's Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Wet (spanning both ends); the page's prose also says the vine 'needs good drainage'. Fast is not supported.

soil_base left null: no admissible source states a potting or bed mix.
water_regime and all watering/fertilizer fields left null: NC State gives drainage tags and a drought-tolerant trait but no watering instruction; this is an in-ground perennial.

Temperature, humidity, light footcandle, chill damage and direct_sun_hours_max left null: no species-specific figure on the readable page (the NC State light legend hours are site-wide, not species prose).
outdoor_sun_exposure uses NC State's Light field (Full sun; Partial Shade 2-6 hours mapped to part_shade).

Size: NC State Dimensions Height 15 ft - 20 ft (180-240 in) and Width 3 ft - 6 ft (36-72 in); the height is for a twining vine that needs a support structure, so it may reflect climbing length rather than free-standing height.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Carum carvi page renders one Common Name(s) list (alphabetized: Caraway, Meridian Fennel, Persian Cumin), and its page-title parenthetical gives the same three names in the same order; common_name 'Caraway' is the first item of both and is the name the Description prose uses. The page lists the previous names Bunium carvi, Carum aromaticum and Carum decussatum. 'Meridian Fennel' is an alias of Carum carvi on this page and must not be confused with Fennel (Foeniculum vulgare): NC State's own Foeniculum vulgare page lists Bronze Fennel, Fennel, Finocchio, Florence Fennel and Sweet Fennel and does not list Meridian Fennel.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Carum carvi page has no Poison block, so it gives no human-scoped severity rating, no symptom list, no poison-part list, no dose and no handling warning. Its Problems field, which is separate from any Poison block, renders three tags: Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. The Tags line reads: #problem for cats #problem for horses #problem for dogs #edible #herbaceous perennial #flowering #herb garden #edible garden #partial shade tolerant #pollinator garden #summer flowers #white flowers #full sun tolerant #bee friendly. Plant Type renders two values: Edible, Herb. The tags give no symptoms, plant parts or amounts, so the cat/dog concern is a bare tag and its cause is unknown. The same page also treats the plant as food. Its Edibility field says: 'Leaves and seeds are typically eaten, but all parts are edible. Seeds have a spicy flavor; leaves are less spicy, with a parsley-dill flavor.' The Description adds that the compound leaves are often used in salads, teas, stews, and soups, that caraway seeds flavor multiple foods, and that the first-year root is edible and can be cooked (no cooking time is given). The page's Tags say 'herbaceous perennial', its Life Cycle field lists both Biennial and Perennial, and its Description calls the plant a biennial. Only NC State could be read, so no second admissible source confirms or contradicts the cat/dog tags or the edibility statement.
unknowns: Only NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) had a readable dedicated page for Carum carvi. RHS returned 404 for the plant URLs tried, Clemson HGIC returned 403, and the Missouri Botanical Garden/plantfinder.mobot.org fetch was denied by the sandbox. No page was found at UF/IFAS or the other admissible domains, and none was retried. Every populated field therefore rests on NC State alone.

Two-year life cycle: NC State's Description calls caraway an 'edible herbaceous biennial', but its Life Cycle field lists both Biennial and Perennial and its Tags line says 'herbaceous perennial', so the page itself is inconsistent. The page does not say in words that seed is harvested in the second year. Its only harvest timing is the Fruit field's Display/Harvest Time of Fall, with Fruit Value To Gardener: Edible. Its Description says the first-year root is edible and can be cooked, and that established plants have deep roots and do not tolerate root disturbance. There is no schema field for life cycle.

toxic_to_pets is true only on NC State's Problems tags (Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs). There is no Poison block, so symptoms, toxic parts, severity and handling are unknown. These tags conflict in spirit with the page's edible status, and the page does not reconcile them. Pet owners should not treat the plant as food for pets on the strength of its human edibility.

soil_drainage moderate comes from NC State's bare Soil Drainage pair 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist' plus the prose 'moist well-drained garden soil'. This is not fast drainage. The Description also says the plant is a good plant for breaking up sub-soil on 'heavy, wet land', and wild habitat is 'moist meadows', so the page is not dry-loving.

water_regime and the water interval fields are null because NC State gives only a soil adjective ('moist well-drained garden soil') and habitat description, with no watering statement or structured moisture field. fertilize_* fields are null because the page has no fertilizing guidance.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max use the Description sentence 'It tolerates a pH in the range 4.8 to 7.6'. The structured Soil pH field lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), which agree but do not alone set bounds. RHS's pH field could not be checked for alkaline tolerance.

outdoor_sun_exposure uses NC State's structured Light field (Full sun 6 or more hours; Partial Shade 2-6 hours, mapped to part_shade) and the prose 'full sun to light shade'. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the hour ranges are the site-wide light-category legend, not species prose. The Description also says plants in full sun are richer in essential oils and more aromatic.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. NC State treats it as an outdoor herb (Plant Type: Edible, Herb; USDA zones 4a-9b); it lists Landscape Location: Container, Small Space, Walkways, and Landscape Theme: Edible Garden, Pollinator Garden, as separate fields, which are outdoor siting, not indoor culture. Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles and chill damage are not stated by NC State, so they are null.

mature_height_in 12-24 and mature_spread_in 10-12 are converted from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 1 ft 0 in to 2 ft 0 in; Width 0 ft 10 in to 1 ft 0 in). The Description says '1 to 2 feet tall and spread 1 foot wide', consistent with the block.
This is the catalog's first Carum. The aliases 'Meridian Fennel' and 'Persian Cumin' are NC State common names for Carum carvi, not Foeniculum vulgare.

records.name_note: Sources differ on the lead name. RHS's dedicated page for Tragopogon porrifolius is titled with 'salsify' and lists 'Jerusalem star, oyster plant, oyster root, purple goat's beard, vegetable oyster' under Other common names. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Common Salsify first, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical), while its description text calls the plant Purple Goat's Beard. 'Oyster Plant' is an alias on this species' pages, but NC State's page for Tradescantia spathacea also lists Oyster Plant; the two are different species and must not be merged. NC State says this species hybridizes with Yellow Goat's Beard (Tragopogon pratensis), a separate species. Salsify was chosen as the lead name.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source gives a poison-part list, symptom list, or cat/dog toxicity statement for this plant, so toxic_to_pets is left null. NC State calls the roots, leaves and flowering shoots edible; older roots should be cooked. NC State's Edibility field says: "The plant's roots and leaves are edible. They taste best if collected before the production of the flower. The roots taste similar to asparagus or oysters. Older roots should be cook, but raw young roots may be grated and used in salads. The flowering shoots can be eaten raw or cooked." (the source's own wording, including its 'should be cook' typo). NC State also says that when the stem is cut or torn it releases a sticky, milky, white sap. RHS says the young root is harvested in its first year and used as a vegetable. NC State also says "The young shoots of the plant may be used like asparagus." and "The roots are best harvested in the late fall and during the winter."
unknowns: No admissible source gives pet toxicity or a poison-part list for salsify; toxic_to_pets left null. NC State shows no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags on this page.

Preparation and timing notes: NC State says roots and leaves taste best collected before flowering, older roots should be cooked, and young roots can be eaten raw. RHS says the young root is harvested in the first year and used as a vegetable, with the edible root harvested in winter. NC State also says roots are best harvested in late fall and winter.

Mature size: NC State has no Dimensions block (its 'Available Space To Plant: 12 inches-3 feet' is not a mature size), so RHS Max Height 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) are used, converted at x39.37. NC State's Quick ID hint says 'up to 4 feet tall' (48 in) and RHS's description says 'up to1.2m tall' (47 in); both exceed RHS's Max Height field.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral. The open-ended bands give no ceiling, and RHS accepts acid soils while NC State omits them.

water_regime left null: RHS's 'Moist but well-drained' is a soil adjective, not a watering statement, and NC State gives only Soil Drainage 'Good Drainage'. No admissible source gives a watering instruction. All water_* and fertilize_* fields are null.
soil_drainage is moderate from RHS's 'Moist but well-drained' moisture field; NC State's bare 'Good Drainage' alone would be ambiguous.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun (6 or more hours) and Partial Shade (2-6 hours); RHS lists Full sun, Partial shade. Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max left null because no species-specific prose gives a maximum.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant; NC State's Plant Type is Edible, Wildflower, with USDA zones 5a-9b. Humidity, temperature, light in foot-candles, chill damage and cool rest are null: no admissible source addresses them for this outdoor biennial. RHS hardiness H4 and NC State zones 5a-9b are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.

Only NC State and RHS were usable. plantfinder.mobot.org was not reachable from the sandbox, the UF/IFAS EDIS salsify publication (mv129) returned HTTP 410, and no dedicated MoBot, Clemson, UMD, PSU or UGA page was found, so no further source was checked.
The RHS and NC State pages are for the species itself, not the genus. Yellow goat's beard (Tragopogon pratensis) is a separate species with its own pages and is not merged here.
The catalog's landed Oyster Plant (Tradescantia spathacea, b96) shares the alias 'Oyster Plant' with this species and must stay a separate record.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State: the page banner says "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics." The Poison Severity (Medium), Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle and Poison Part fields sit in the page's "Poisonous to Humans" block, so that severity rating is human-scoped. Poison Part: Seeds. Poison Symptoms: "Nausea, headache, hallucinations, vomiting, convulsions, and coma if the seeds are eaten in large amounts." Poison Toxic Principle: "Terpene peroxide ascaridole and others". Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Separately, the Landscape "Problems" tags are: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy (these cat/dog/horse tags are separate from the human Poison block and carry no symptom list). Plant Type values: Annual, Perennial, Poisonous, Weed. The page's tag line reads "#heat tolerant #full sun tolerant #spreading #poisonous #problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats #high maintenance #wind pollinated #self-seeding #fast growing #fragrant leaves #short-lived perennials #tropical #annual #deer resistant #fragrant flowers #weedy". The page gives no handling warning. The description adds: "The plant was used to help remove intestinal worms but the dose needed can be toxic." Leaf edibility is a separate statement: "Leaves are used in teas and as a leafy green and in various Mexican dishes."; the description adds "The leaves are also used in Mexican dishes and helps to negate the gas-causing effects of beans." The seeds are the only listed poison part; the leaves are the only part NC State calls food. NC State gives no preparation times or conditions for eating the leaves, and no other admissible source was available to confirm or contradict the scope.

records.toxicity_detail: From NC State's dedicated Taraxacum officinale page: the page header says the plant has low severity poison characteristics, and its "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped) gives Poison Severity: Low, Poison Symptoms: Skin irritation after exposure to sap., Poison Toxic Principle: Taraxinic acid, Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. The page names no poisonous plant part (it only attributes the irritation to the sap) and has no cat/dog tag. Separate "Problems" tags on the page: Contact Dermatitis, Weedy. Plant Type tags: Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Weed, Wildflower (the description calls it an edible, herbaceous perennial wildflower or weed in the daisy family). Edibility field: "Leaves and flowers are used in salads and stir-fries as well as jams, wines, and teas. Young leaves are best for raw eating and older leaves are better cooked. Roots are roasted and used as a coffee alternative." The description adds that the milky latex sap has also been used medicinally. Landscape Location: Lawn, Naturalized Area; the description says it is not generally cultivated in the home landscape but, left to grow in lawns and naturalized areas, provides a bright accent. Young leaves are best for raw eating and older leaves are better cooked (a preference, not a restriction). The sap causes skin irritation; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Only NC State was reachable, so no second source confirms or disputes scope or edibility.
